passage: Diwali week, and the family group had dozens of unread messages before breakfast. Most were forwards about the election, with my uncle Pankaj's angry replies stacked underneath. I love these people, and my shoulders still tightened every time the phone buzzed. This year I tried something small. I wrote, "Happy Diwali everyone! New rule from me: no forwards, please, just photos and sweets 🙂" Then I called Pankaj Uncle and asked about his morning walks, and he talked for ten minutes without mentioning politics once. When a video arrived that night, I checked it first, found it was old, and told only him, privately. I muted the group for the evening without announcing it. Nobody fell out. — Hrithik

qa.q: What did Hrithik write in the family group as a new rule?
qa.a: Hrithik asked for "no forwards, please, just photos and sweets."

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's shoulders tighten whenever the phone buzzed?
qa.a: Hrithik loves the family but is worn out by the steady political forwards. The tight shoulders are a cue of that tiredness, and the love is still there.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try if another doubtful video is shared in the group?
qa.a: Check it first, and if it is wrong, tell the sender privately instead of arguing in front of everyone, as was done with Pankaj.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when Hrithik phoned and asked about his morning walks?
qa.a: He probably felt cared about and listened to, since he talked for ten minutes without bringing up politics.

grounding: Shows gentle rules in a family group during a festival: no forwards, checking before sharing, changing the subject warmly and muting quietly.

passage:
Before. Two days before Diwali, the Sharma family group had 214 unread messages. Swati scrolled: sweet recipes, a baby photo, then a forwarded video about the opposition, then three uncles arguing in capital letters. Her cousin Ojas had left the group once already. She put the phone down, tired to her bones.

During. On Diwali morning, a new forward arrived claiming a minister had banned firecrackers nationwide. Swati checked; it was false. She typed carefully: "Happy Diwali, everyone! 🪔 Small request: can we keep this group for family news and photos, and check before forwarding? Love you all." Then she posted a picture of Dadi's rangoli.

After. A week later, the group was calmer. One uncle still sent forwards now and then; Swati replied with a photo of her dinner and moved on. Ojas messaged her privately: "Rejoined. It's nice again." She grinned and muted only the uncle's late-night videos.

qa.q: How many unread messages did the family group have two days before Diwali?
How did Swati feel as she scrolled the group before Diwali?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and weary, loving her family but worn out by the arguments and forwards.

qa.q: Which of Swati's gentle rules worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking warmly to keep the group for family news and to check before forwarding worked, because it set a limit without shaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Ojas see the change in the group?
qa.a: Ojas seems relieved and glad, rejoining because the group felt "nice again".

grounding: Across three days, the passage shows a young woman who loves her family but is tired of political forwards, setting gentle rules and changing the subject warmly.

passage:
"Anirban, put the phone down for a minute and listen to your old aunt.

When I was twenty-five, we didn't have phone groups. We had Holi lunch at your great-grandfather's house, forty people and one long table. Every year the men argued about elections until someone cried. I loved them all and I dreaded that lunch.

One year I, Vidya, the youngest daughter-in-law, did something new. When your grandfather started on the ruling party, I stood up and said, 'Papa, no politics till the gujiyas are finished. Tell us about your first Holi instead.' Everyone laughed. He told the story. Nobody fought.

I did it every year after that. They called it Vidya's rule.

So when your family group gets noisy, beta, you don't need to win. Change the subject kindly. It works better than you'd think."

qa.q: What did Vidya ask Papa to talk about instead of politics?
What did Vidya feel about the Holi lunch before that year?
qa.a: She loved everyone there but dreaded the lunch, because the arguments always ended with someone crying.

qa.q: Which choice at the Holi lunch changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Vidya standing up to warmly change the subject worked, because it was light and loving, not a scolding, so everyone laughed and joined in.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father-in-law have seen her interruption?
qa.a: He may have felt honoured to be asked for his story, which is why he told it instead of arguing.

grounding: An elder recalls being tired of family political fights at festivals and setting a warm rule to change the subject, which kept love and peace at the table.
